newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin faces test on Europe this month.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin faces test on Europe this month.

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will get an early chance to test his new Socialist-led government's policies on Europe at a series of international gatherings in the next two weeks.
He has avoided policy statements since a parliamentary election swept him to power last Sunday on a pledge to resist further austerity dictated by crtiteria for greater European economic integration.

But financial markets are watching closely to see whether he will stick to a campaign pledge to renegotiate the European Union's "stability pact" meant to limit budget deficits after the planned launch of the euro single currency at the beginning of 1999.
The pact was due to have been nodded through by heads of state at an EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 and then adopted formally by the 15-nation group's finance ministers.

Asked whether Jospin would block its approval in Amsterdam, and whether he would accompany President Jacques Chirac to the summit, government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said it was for the prime minister to say.

The German daily newspaper Die Zeit quoted former European Commission president Jacques Delors, a Socialist close to Jospin, as saying he did not believe the premier wanted to water down the pact, seen by Germany as a vital guarantee of a solid euro.
Delors, who endorsed Jospin's European credentials during the campaign, also warned against delay in the single currency's launch.
But Jospin may find it hard to back down on his party's call for new talks on the stability pact so soon after taking office.

Meanwhile his is due to have intensive contacts with other European leaders, beginning with a meeting of Socialist leaders in Malmo, Sweden, on Friday, to spell out and refine the party's position on Europe.
He will address the conference on Friday and hold talks with Britain's new prime minister, Tony Blair, whose Labour Party ended 18 years of Conservative rule on May 1 with a landslide election win.

The French Socialists have also called for a flexible reading of the 1991 Maastricht treaty on European integration, immediate membership in economic and monetary union for Italy and Spain, a European economic government and a euro that is not overvalued against the dollar.

Jospin told reporters on Thursday he planned to attend a Franco-German summit in Poitiers, western France, on June 13, along with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Chirac and senior French and German ministers.
Olivier Schrameck, head of Jospin's private office, said the premier would be making contact with his counterparts abroad but declined to say if he would see Kohl before Poitiers.
"I confirm that the prime minister will have contacts with his counterparts, notably his European counterparts," Schrameck told a news conference.
Germany, France's key ally in building monetary union, is watching to see how hard the new French government wants to bargain on Europe.

Bonn has its own problems with meeting the budget deficit and debt criteria for the single currency and has just suffered a setback at the hands of the Bundesbank on the issue by agreeing under pressure to delay revaluing German gold reserves.

Before the French election, which forced Chirac into sharing power with a government made up of opposition parties, Chirac and Kohl were seen as joint guarantors of the monetary union project going ahead on time.
Trautmann declined to say whether Jospin would accompany Chirac to every international summit.
"It is a question on which there will be a discussion between the president and the prime minister in the interests of the republic and the nation," she said.

In the absence of any policy statements, Jospin's decision on whether on not to join Chirac at international meetings is being watched for an indication of how much he plans to push the Socialist party line on Europe.
